entry: Rail transport system with capacity greater than [[Light rail|light rail]] but less than [[Rapid transit|rapid transit]]. Such systems typically have shorter trains and smaller stations than rapid transit and run on entirely grade-separated rights of way. Automatic train operation allows some to reach peak-hour headways as close as 90 seconds. A World Bank report places their capacity at 15,000 to 30,000 passengers per hour per direction.

[[Iron Age]] civilization of western [[Anatolia]], centered on its capital, Sardis. Lydia is credited with the world's first coinage, and its [[Electrum|electrum]] coins, dated to around the 7th century BC, are among the oldest in existence. Under Alyattes and [[Croesus]] its military power extended Lydian control over all of Asia Minor west of the River Halys, except Lycia. In 546 BC it became a satrapy of the [[Achaemenid Empire]], and in 133 BC part of the Roman province of Asia. The Lydian language, an Indo-European tongue related to Luwian and Hittite, became extinct in the 1st century BC. The ancient [[Tumulus|burial mounds]] at Bin Tepe are among the largest on Earth. Primary accounts come from [[Herodotus]] and from the Lydian historian Xanthus, author of the *Lydiaca*, which survives only in fragments.

Sixteenth-century Spanish maritime expedition that was the first to circumnavigate the Earth. Planned by Portuguese explorer [[Ferdinand Magellan]], it left [[Spain]] in 1519 to seek a western route to the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, in present-day [[Indonesia]]. Magellan died in battle in the Philippines in April 1521, and [[Juan Sebastián Elcano]] led the expedition's return to Spain in September 1522. Only 18 men and one ship, the *Victoria*, completed the circumnavigation, and the voyage had endured mutinies, starvation and [[Scurvy|scurvy]]. The fleet passed through the [[Strait of Magellan]] in November 1520 and crossed the Pacific in 98 days, the first crossing of that ocean by a European expedition. The route was much longer and harder than expected and was not commercially useful, yet the voyage is regarded as one of the greatest achievements in seamanship.

South African all-female vocal group specializing in mbaqanga. Formed in 1964, the group combined multi-part harmonies with the baritone vocals of Simon Nkabinde, known as Mahlathini, and backing by the Makgona Tsohle Band. Tours took the group across neighboring countries. Its upbeat music offered listeners respite during the [[Apartheid|apartheid]] era. Its international breakthrough came in the 1980s through [[Paul Simon]]'s album *Graceland* and a performance at [[Nelson Mandela]]'s 70th birthday concert. Hilda Tloubatla, the original soprano, remains in the current line-up with Amanda Nkosi and Nqobile Njapha.

Island country in the central [[Mediterranean Sea]] (pop., 2024: 574,250). Its two main islands are Malta and [[Gozo]], with the capital at [[Valletta]]; because it consists of a single urban region, it is often described as a [[City-state|city-state]]. The island of Malta has been inhabited since at least 6500 BC and was later ruled by [[Phoenicia|Phoenicians]], Romans, Arabs and Normans, then by the [[Knights Hospitaller]] and the French before British rule as a crown colony in the early 19th century. It was besieged by the Axis powers during [[World War II]] and was an Allied base. It gained independence in 1964, established a parliamentary republic in 1974, and joined the [[European Union]] in 2004. Catholicism is the state religion, although the constitution guarantees freedom of religion. The economy is advanced and high-income, and heavily reliant on tourism.

French-Spanish musician. He sings in French, Spanish, English, Italian, Arabic, Catalan, Galician, Portuguese, Greek and others. He began his career busking in [[Paris]]. Influenced by the UK rock scene, particularly [[The Clash]], he and other musicians formed the rockabilly group Hot Pants in the mid-1980s. In 1987 he co-founded Mano Negra with his brother Antoine; the band achieved considerable success in Europe before breaking up in 1995. As a solo artist he has toured regularly with his live band, Radio Bemba Sound System.

Systematic transformation of a [[Sphere|sphere]] or ellipsoid, such as the [[Earth]], onto a plane. All projections distort the surface in some way, so each preserves some properties, such as area, shape, direction or distance, at the expense of others. The best-known is the [[Mercator projection]], which is conformal but enlarges regions far from the equator; critics have faulted it for this throughout the 20th century. Equal-area projections, such as the [[Gall–Peters projection]], show the correct sizes of countries relative to each other but distort angles. The National Geographic Society and most atlases favor compromise projections that balance area and angular distortion, such as the Robinson projection. A [[United Nations]] resolution, with 164 countries voting in favor, recognized the distortions inherent to the Mercator projection and promoted equal-area projections, notably the Equal Earth projection. The [[United States]] was the only country to vote against it.

Latvian-born American abstract painter. He is best known for [[Color field|color field]] paintings of rectangular color regions, produced from 1949, though he did not subscribe to any one school. Born into a Jewish family in [[Daugavpils]], then part of the [[Russian Empire]], he immigrated to the United States, arriving at [[Ellis Island]] in late 1913. He moved to [[New York City]] in 1923, where his early work dealt primarily with urban scenery. In the 1940s, responding to [[World War II]], he experimented with mythological themes and Surrealism to express tragedy. He refunded the commission for the Seagram murals, intended for a restaurant, and donated the paintings to museums, including the Tate Gallery. He contributed 14 canvases to the non-denominational Rothko Chapel in [[Houston]], Texas.

[[Florence|Florentine]] painter of the early [[Italian Renaissance]]. According to Vasari, he was the best painter of his generation because of his skill at imitating nature, and he is regarded as the first great Italian painter of the Quattrocento. He was among the first to use [[Perspective (graphical)|linear perspective]] and to employ the vanishing point in art for the first time, and he moved from the elaborate ornamentation of [[Gentile da Fabriano]] toward a naturalism that used [[Chiaroscuro|chiaroscuro]] for greater realism. The earliest works attributed to him include *San Giovenale Triptych* (1422) and *Virgin and Child with Saint Anne* (c. 1424) at the [[Uffizi]]. His innovations influenced later artists, including [[Michelangelo]], who studied his Brancacci Chapel frescoes in Florence. Despite a brief career, his influence was profound; little is known about the circumstances of his death, and on hearing of it, [[Filippo Brunelleschi]] said, "We have suffered a great loss."

American multinational [[Fast food|fast-food]] restaurant chain. Founded in 1940 as a restaurant operated by brothers [[Richard and Maurice McDonald]] in San Bernardino, California, it grew into one of the world's largest restaurant chains. In 1948 the brothers introduced the Speedee Service System, which simplified the menu to nine items. At the end of 2025 it had 45,356 restaurants in more than 100 countries, approximately 95% of them operated by [[Franchising|franchisees]]. Businessman [[Ray Kroc]] became a franchise agent in 1955 and bought the brothers' stake in 1961, overseeing its domestic and international expansion. The menu centers on [[Hamburger|hamburgers]] and [[French fries]], with the [[Big Mac]] among its best-known products. The company has faced criticism over the nutritional content of its food, its treatment of animals, its environmental impact, and employee wages and working conditions.

Female monster in Greek mythology, one of the three [[Gorgons]]. She is generally described as a woman with living snakes in place of hair, and anyone who looked at her was turned to stone. Of the three sisters, only Medusa was mortal, and the hero [[Perseus]] beheaded her. He then used her head, which still turned onlookers to stone, as a weapon until he gave it to the goddess [[Athena]], who placed it on her shield. Pegasus, a winged horse, and the giant Chrysaor sprang from her body when she was beheaded. Hesiod and [[Aeschylus]] located her on Sarpedon near Cisthene, while [[Herodotus]] associated the Gorgons with [[Libya]]. In classical antiquity her head appeared on the evil-averting device known as the Gorgoneion. [[Ovid]] also said that the corals of the [[Red Sea]] formed from Medusa's blood.

Family of [[Biomolecule|biomolecules]] organized as oligomers or polymers, providing pigment in many organisms. It is produced in specialized cells called melanocytes through a process in which the oxidation of the amino acid [[Tyrosine|tyrosine]] is followed by polymerization. There are five basic types: eumelanin, pheomelanin, neuromelanin, allomelanin and pyomelanin. Eumelanin, which is dark brown or black, is an effective absorber of [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light and is thought to protect skin cells from radiation damage; pheomelanin is largely responsible for the red or yellow tints of some skin and hair. Neuromelanin, found in the brain, has been investigated for its efficacy in treating neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's. Disrupted melanin production underlies disorders such as [[Albinism|albinism]] and [[Vitiligo|vitiligo]]. Exposure to UV radiation is associated with an increased risk of [[Melanoma|melanoma]], a cancer of melanocytes.

Guidance relationship between an experienced person and a less experienced one. The word was inspired by Mentor, a character in [[Homer]]'s epic poem in which the goddess [[Athena]] assumes his appearance to guide young Telemachus. A mentor need not be senior to the person mentored; what matters is experience that others can learn from. Mentoring in Europe existed as early as [[Ancient Greece]], and since the 1970s it has spread in the United States, mainly in [[Training|training]] contexts.

Experiment from 1887 to detect the motion of the [[Earth]] through the [[Luminiferous aether|luminiferous aether]]. [[Albert A. Michelson]] and [[Edward W. Morley]] performed it between April and July 1887 at what is now Case Western Reserve University in [[Cleveland]], Ohio. It compared the speed of light in perpendicular directions and found no significant difference, a null result generally considered the first strong evidence against some aether theories. The result helped lead to [[Special relativity|special relativity]], which rules out motion against an aether. Repeated experiments with greater sensitivity, including one in 2009 that found no aether wind at the 10−17 level, are among the fundamental tests of special relativity.

Buddhist mountain and scenic site in Chizhou, [[Anhui|Anhui]] Province, [[China]]. It is one of China's four famous Buddhist mountains and one of the first batch of 5A-level scenic spots. A legend credits the Tang poet [[Li Bai]] with naming it; the name means Nine Glorious Mountains. In 719 Kim Qiaoque, a [[Silla]] prince ordained as a [[Bhikkhu|bhikkhu]], arrived; the community believed him an incarnation of Dizang Bodhisattva, and the mountain became dedicated to Dizang. During the Ming and Qing dynasties it had as many as 360 temples.

Fine-grained siliciclastic [[Sedimentary rock|sedimentary rock]] with at least 50% mud-sized particles. Mudrocks make up about half of the sedimentary rocks in the geologic record and are easily the most widespread deposits on Earth. Varieties include [[Siltstone|siltstone]], claystone, mudstone and [[Shale|shale]], the last of which splits readily into thin layers. Scientists accept more than one classification scheme, and mudrocks are difficult to study because of their small grains and susceptibility to [[Weathering|weathering]]. They have been important since the beginning of civilization, when pottery and mudbricks were made by hand.

Branch of [[Science|science]] concerned with the description, understanding and prediction of natural phenomena, based on empirical evidence from observation and experimentation. It divides into life science, alternatively known as [[Biology|biology]], and physical science, which includes [[Physics|physics]], astronomy, Earth science and [[Chemistry|chemistry]]. As empirical science, it uses tools from the formal sciences, such as [[Mathematics|mathematics]] and logic, to convert information about nature into measurements explained as clear statements of the laws of nature. Modern natural science succeeded classical [[Natural philosophy|natural philosophy]]; [[Galileo Galilei]], [[Isaac Newton]] and others debated whether mathematical or experimental methods were better for investigating nature. Mechanisms such as peer review and reproducibility help ensure the validity of advances.

[[Subset|Subset]] of a [[Topological space|topological space]] containing an open set around a given point. Intuitively, one can move some distance in any direction from the point without leaving the neighborhood. A set that is a neighborhood of each of its points is [[Open set|open]], and the neighborhood system at a point is the collection of all its neighborhoods. In a [[Metric space|metric space]], a set is a neighborhood of a point if it contains an open ball of some positive radius around that point.

Branch of [[Chemistry|chemistry]] dealing with radioactivity, nuclear processes and transformations in atomic nuclei. It covers the chemistry of radioactive elements such as the [[Actinide|actinides]], [[Radium]] and radon, and the behavior of materials in nuclear reactors and waste storage sites. It also studies how radiation alters biochemicals within living organisms, which aids understanding of medical treatments such as [[Cancer|cancer]] radiotherapy. Radioactive tracers are used in industry and the environment, and nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy aids structural analysis. After X-rays were discovered in 1895, [[Henri Becquerel]] found that uranium emitted rays without an external energy source, and [[Marie Curie|Marie Skłodowska-Curie]] and Pierre Curie isolated polonium and radium. [[Ernest Rutherford]] showed that radioactive decay can be described by a simple equation, implying a characteristic [[Half-life|half-life]] for each radioactive substance.

Reaction in which the nucleus of an [[Atom|atom]] splits into two or more smaller nuclei. The energy released by the fission of one [[Uranium-235|uranium-235]] atom is about 100 million times that released by burning one carbon atom in air. [[Otto Hahn]] and Fritz Strassmann demonstrated fission in December 1938, and [[Lise Meitner]] and Otto Robert Frisch explained it theoretically in January 1939; Frisch named the process by analogy with the biological fission of living cells. Hahn and Strassmann predicted that fission releases additional neutrons, opening the possibility of a [[Chain reaction|chain reaction]] in a critical mass of fissile material. Three isotopes, U-233, U-235 and Pu-239, can sustain a chain reaction, allowing [[Nuclear reactor|nuclear reactors]] a controllable energy release and [[Nuclear weapon|nuclear weapons]] an uncontrolled one within about a microsecond.

Class of large [[Biomolecule|biomolecules]] essential to all known life. They are built from [[Nucleotide|nucleotides]], each consisting of a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The two main classes are [[DNA|deoxyribonucleic acid]] and [[RNA|ribonucleic acid]]; they differ in their sugar, [[Deoxyribose|deoxyribose]] in DNA and ribose in RNA. DNA forms a chain of base pairs that stores coded instructions as genes, while RNA usually forms a chain of single bases that helps make proteins. In 1953 [[James Watson]] and [[Francis Crick]] proposed the double-helix structure of DNA. Friedrich Miescher partly discovered nucleic acid in 1869 at the [[University of Tübingen]], and in 1944 the Avery–MacLeod–McCarty experiment showed that DNA carries genetic information.

Hardwood tree or shrub of the genus *Quercus*, in the beech family. Oaks have spirally arranged leaves, often lobed, and bear acorns borne within a cup; the genus has some 475 species, both deciduous and evergreen. Oaks are [[Keystone species|keystone species]] in habitats from Mediterranean semi-desert to subtropical [[Rainforest|rainforest]], and they support more than 950 species of [[Caterpillar|caterpillar]]. Oak leaves and acorns contain enough [[Tannin|tannin]] to be toxic to [[Cattle|cattle]], though pigs can digest them safely. Oak timber is strong and hard and is used in construction and [[Furniture|furniture]]-making. Wine barrels are made of oak and are used to age sherry and [[Whisky|whisky]]. Almost a third of oak species are threatened with extinction from climate change, invasive pests and habitat loss. In culture, the oak symbolizes strength and is the national tree of many countries.

Legendary Greek king of Ithaca and hero of [[Homer]]'s epic. In [[Latin]] he is known as Ulysses. He is renowned for guile and versatility, and Homer calls him *polytropos*, meaning the man of many turns. He was a key leader among the Greek forces in the [[Trojan War]] and is credited with devising the [[Trojan Horse]] stratagem that enabled the fall of [[Troy]]. His ten-year *nostos*, or homecoming, took him past the [[Siren (mythology)|Sirens]] and the Cyclops Polyphemus; [[Athena]] guided him and [[Hermes]] aided him on the island of Aeaea. He returned to Ithaca disguised as a beggar, killed the suitors who had overrun his palace, and was reunited with Penelope.

[[International organization]] founded in 1948 to promote cooperation among member states in the [[Americas]]. According to the Council on Foreign Relations, it is a voluntary multilateral regional body focused on human rights, electoral oversight, social and economic development, and security in the [[Western Hemisphere]]. Its origins lie in the First International Conference of American States (1889–1890), at which 18 nations resolved to found the International Union of American Republics. In the 19th century [[José de San Martín]] and [[Simón Bolívar]] proposed a league of American republics at the 1826 Congress of Panama. Supporters credit the organization with advancing the rule of law and electoral integrity, while critics point to its dependence on funding from the [[United States]]. Albert Ramdin of [[Suriname]] was inaugurated as secretary general in May 2025, replacing Luis Almagro of Uruguay.

Series of mountain ranges along the Pacific coast of [[North America]]. They run from [[Alaska]] south to northern and central Mexico and form part of the North American [[American Cordillera|Cordillera]]. In California they are an accretionary wedge formed by eastward subduction of the [[Farallon plate]] during the Mesozoic. Their character varies from tidewater glaciers in Alaska to the [[Chaparral|chaparral]]-covered ranges of Southern California. In winter, cool unstable air masses from the [[Gulf of Alaska]] often bring heavy rain and snow to western slopes north of San Francisco Bay. Along the coasts of [[British Columbia]] and Alaska, mountains meet the sea in a maze of [[Fjord|fjords]] and thousands of islands.
